analysis.one_liner: Creates a licensing and disclosure system for paid tax preparers and refund-advance products.
analysis.headline: The bill, aimed at protecting tax filers from bad preparers and costly refund advances, never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Treasury Department certify tax return preparers, decertify or penalize incompetent or dishonest ones, and require preparers to disclose their fees and warn customers about refund anticipation payment arrangements — short-term advances on tax refunds sold by preparers and lenders. It would also let Treasury charge preparers annual fees to cover testing and oversight. The bill was introduced in the House in September 2021, sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and no further action was taken before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tax filers who pay for return preparation — especially low- and moderate-income households that use refund anticipation products — would gain protections against preparers who misfile returns, hide fees, or sell costly advances on refunds that are not necessary to receive their money.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would authorize Treasury to certify tax return preparers, require them to demonstrate competency and good character, and decertify, censure, or penalize those who are incompetent or who willfully mislead customers [S2][S3].

It would require preparers to disclose their fees for preparation and filing, explain how long a normal IRS direct deposit takes, and state that a refund anticipation payment arrangement is not necessary to receive a tax refund [S3].

It would warn customers that if their refund is smaller or later than expected, they may still owe the fees and interest on a refund advance, and it would let Treasury fine preparers up to $1,000 per failure to disclose [S3].
It would let Treasury impose penalties on preparer firms themselves when they knew or should have known of a preparer's misconduct, capped at the gross income derived from the conduct [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation chains, storefront preparers, and the banks and lenders that issue refund anticipation advances would bear new certification fees, testing costs, and fines, and would face disclosure rules that could cut sales of refund-advance products.

drawbacks.text: The bill would add new licensing, testing, and annual fees for preparers, costs that small independent preparers might struggle to absorb and could pass to customers in higher prices [S3].

Decades of similar proposals have drawn objections that competency testing could push some volunteer and low-cost preparers out of the market, leaving some filers fewer options; the bill's own text acknowledges fee coverage for 'competency testing and training' [S3].

Disclosure mandates address the refund-advance problem only indirectly: customers would still be able to buy advances, and a disclosure-only remedy relies on customers reading and acting on fine print.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a consumer-protection measure aimed at a market with documented abuses — preparers who misfile returns and lenders who sell refund advances at high effective cost to people who could simply wait a week or two for direct deposit. The costs are regulatory burdens on preparers and lenders, some of which could reach consumers through higher prep fees. The disclosure approach is a middle path: it informs customers rather than banning the products outright, which means some of the harm it targets may persist.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote, so the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on September 27, 2021, joined by Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee [S1][S3][S5].
Two Democratic members cosponsored the bill, and no action beyond the referral appears in the legislative record [S4][S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a companion Senate action, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax preparation chains and refund-advance lenders are better off because the bill never advanced: the certification regime and disclosure mandates that would have pressured their products never took effect, and filers were left with no new protections.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the Ways and Means Committee

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote before the Congress ended

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote in the roughly 15 months after introduction

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no floor positions were recorded; the only members on record as supporting the bill were its two Democratic sponsors, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Tax preparation chains and storefront preparers
industries.note: The bill would require these firms to be certified and tested, disclose fees, and face fines up to $1,000 per undisclosed item, with firm-level penalties for knowing misconduct. The bill died, so none of these rules took effect.

industries.industry: Refund-advance lenders and their partner banks
industries.note: Refund anticipation products — advances on tax refunds sold at a fee or interest — would have faced mandatory disclosures telling customers the advance is unnecessary, how long a normal refund takes, and that they may still owe fees if the refund is short. Disclosure rules of this kind tend to shrink sales of these products, which profit from customers who cannot or do not wait for their refund.
